title: Send a change by email: format-patch and am
summary: How the Linux kernel and every mailing-list project work. Export commits as patch files, apply them on another machine, and keep the original author's name on the commit.
mental_model: `format-patch` writes each commit as an mbox-format file containing the author, date, message and diff. `git am` reads those files back and recreates the commits — including their original authorship, which plain `git apply` cannot do.

commit.message: Read the sensor properly instead of returning zero

steps.title: Export the contributor's commits as patches
steps.why: Run from the contributor's clone: `format-patch` writes one numbered file per commit. Each is a complete, self-describing unit — author, date, message, diff — that can travel by any means at all.

steps.title: Read one
steps.why: It is an email. From, Date, Subject, the message body, then a unified diff and a git version trailer. Nothing proprietary — that is why this workflow predates and outlives every forge.
steps.expect: A From: line naming Priya, and the commit message as the Subject.

steps.title: Apply them in the maintainer's clone
steps.why: `git am` recreates both commits. Note it takes the files in order and creates one commit per patch — this is a replay, not a squash.
steps.expect: Two new commits, and the driver code updated.

verify.label: both patches applied as separate commits

steps.title: Check who the commits belong to
steps.why: The author is Priya; the committer is you. Git tracks these separately, and `am` preserves the distinction — which is the entire point of using it rather than copying the diff by hand.
steps.expect: author=Priya, committer=Learner on the applied commits.

verify.label: the original author is preserved
verify.hint: git am keeps authorship; git apply would not

verify.label: …while you are recorded as the committer

steps.title: Compare with plain apply
steps.why: `git apply` only touches the working tree — no commit, no author, no message. It is for applying a diff, not for accepting a contribution.
steps.expect: The file changes, but no commit exists and no author was recorded.

steps.title: Back to am, and handle a failure
steps.why: If a patch does not apply, `am` stops with the mbox half-consumed. `--3way` lets git use blob information to merge instead of applying blindly; `--abort` unwinds the whole series.

steps.title: Add a cover letter for a series
steps.why: `--cover-letter` generates a 0000 file describing the whole series with a diffstat. On a mailing list it is the pull-request description — the place you explain why, not what.
steps.expect: A cover letter plus the two patches.

verify.label: the contributor's two commits were applied
verify.hint: git format-patch in their clone, git am in yours

verify.label: authorship was preserved through the patch exchange
both changes are present in the code
clean tree, no am in progress

pitfalls: `git apply` does not commit and does not record an author. Use `git am` for anything you are accepting from someone else.
A failed `am` leaves the series half-applied. `git am --abort` unwinds it; `git am --skip` drops the current patch.
`format-patch <ref>` exports everything since that ref, not just the last commit. Check the file count before sending.
Patches carry no merge information, so a series that depended on a merge cannot be exported faithfully.
cheatsheet: one .patch file per commit since ref
